title: Validate Endpoints with a Result Type
oneLiner: Parse host:port settings into a Result that is either an endpoint or a clear error message, then validate a whole list and report every bad line at once instead of stopping at the first.
keyTakeaway: When bad input is expected, return a result instead of throwing: the caller sees success or a specific reason, and nothing is thrown in the loop. Results also make it natural to collect every error in one pass, which is what users of a config file or form want.
explanation:
Write two functions. ParseEndpoint(text) turns "host:port" into an Endpoint(Host, Port), splitting at the last colon, and returns a Result: Ok with the endpoint, or an error with one of these messages, checked in this order: "missing port" when there's no colon; "empty host" when nothing comes before it; "port is not a number" when the part after it is empty or contains anything but the digits 0 to 9; "port out of range" when the number isn't between 1 and 65535. So "plc-1:502" is fine, "hmi:http" isn't a number and "c:-1" isn't a number either (the minus sign isn't a digit).

ParseAll(lines) parses every line and returns Ok with the list of all endpoints if every line is fine, or an error listing every bad line, numbered from 1, joined by "; ": "line 2: missing port; line 4: port out of range". The checker reports each line's result ("host:port" or "error: message") and then ParseAll's verdict ("ok: N" or "errors: ...").

The Result and Endpoint types are provided. In C#: Result<T>.Ok(value) and Result<T>.Fail(error), with IsOk, Value and Error properties, and record Endpoint(string Host, int Port). In Python: Ok(value) and Err(error) dataclasses, and Endpoint(host, port); match result: case Ok(value): ... case Err(error): ... tells them apart. Watch for numbers too big for an int in C#: check the length or use long, or int.TryParse failing will look like "not a number".

testCases.expectedJson: [["error: missing port", "error: empty host", "error: port is not a number", "error: port out of range"], "errors: line 1: missing port; line 2: empty host; line 3: port is not a number; line 4: port out of range"]
[["error: port out of range", "b:65535", "error: port is not a number"], "errors: line 1: port out of range; line 3: port is not a number"]

[["error: port is not a number", "opc.tcp:4840", "error: port is not a number", "error: port out of range"], "errors: line 1: port is not a number; line 3: port is not a number; line 4: port out of range"]
[["hist:8080", "hist:8080", "error: port is not a number", "hist:80"], "errors: line 3: port is not a number"]

Because each line returned a result, ParseAll could check them all and report every problem at once.

complexity.note: Each line is scanned a constant number of times (find the colon, check the digits, parse), so the whole input of n characters is O(n); the endpoints and error messages take O(n) space.
